Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (health centers) in Rwanda predominantly use digital systems for patient data recording. OpenMRS EMR modules are deployed in nearly 400 of ~500 health centers (2018 baseline), primarily for HIV/TB but expanding, functioning as point-of-care local systems.Rwanda Digital Health Strategy National rollout of integrated EMR (eBuzima) ongoing via MoH partnerships with NGOs like Health Builders in rural districts (e.g., Rwamagana, Rulindo), replacing paper-based records and improving accuracy in pilots.Health Builders Report DHIS2 HMIS collects aggregates nationwide since 2012, supported by revised registers.DHIS2 2022 survey at 54 rural health centers shows high EMR acceptability/use despite some infrastructure issues and possible dual paper entry.JMIR Study Barriers: connectivity/power outages (25% sites), low digital literacy, resistance to change; addressed via training, local servers. National policy targets 100% EMR coverage by 2022, with recent (2025) district rollouts indicating majority digital at POC, though some paper fallback persists in rollout gaps.

revision_notes: Original score of 3 rested on a 2018 EMR baseline and a 2022 JMIR pilot of 54 health centres; a larger, more rigorous 2024 nationwide cross-sectional assessment of 215 health centres found only 33% (71/215) had any EMR system deployed, and just 53.6% of health-centre staff reported active EMR use, indicating paper remains dominant at most rural health centres. The 2025 e-Ubuzima rollout was operating in only 15 of 30 districts as of April 2025, with hardware/connectivity gaps cited as barriers to the government's own end-2025 nationwide target. Score revised down to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) to reflect facility-level reality rather than national policy ambition.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (health centres) in Rwanda are transitioning towards electronic medical records, but paper remains the dominant means of data capture at most facilities. A 2024 nationwide cross-sectional assessment of 215 health centres found that only around a third had any EMR system deployed, with just over half of staff at facilities with EMR access reporting regular use; common barriers include unreliable internet, intermittent electricity, and limited computer access. The Ministry of Health's e-Ubuzima platform, intended to replace paper registers nationwide, was operating in only 15 of Rwanda's 30 districts as of April 2025, with full national rollout (requiring computers and connectivity at all roughly 520 health centres) targeted for end-2025 but not yet achieved. Digital systems such as DHIS2 collect aggregate data nationally, and pockets of point-of-care digitisation exist (for example HIV/TB modules and cervical cancer screening), but daily clinical record-keeping at the majority of rural health centres continues to rely primarily on paper registers supplemented by partial digital systems.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rwanda National Police (RNP) has undergone sustained digital transformation extending to rural areas. The Integrated Electronic Case Management System (IECMS), launched January 2016, covers the entire justice chain — police (Criminal Investigation Department), NPPA, judiciary, and correctional services. 100% of cases are filed electronically, reducing average processing time from 7 to 3.4 months. The IECMS was specifically designed to reach rural areas: a 2023 University of Rwanda dissertation studied its effectiveness in Nyaruguru District, a remote rural area, confirming deployment there. Government has subsidised internet connectivity at 45 rural and remote police sites. SMS notifications allow citizens to track case progress using basic mobile phones. In December 2025, RNP introduced four new online reporting systems. Criminal records are fully digitalised via the Irembo platform. However, ICT literacy gaps and infrastructure limitations remain significant obstacles for rural personnel. Internet penetration stands at ~31%. Some rural stations may still use paper for initial documentation before entering cases into IECMS. Rwanda is categorically different from most African countries — the default is digital, not paper, making it score 3.

A May 2025 Rwanda National Police feature confirms extensive digitisation of policing functions nationwide (driver testing/licensing 90-99% digital via Irembo, automated speed cameras and digital fines raising traffic-enforcement digital capacity to 85%, top-tier ITU cybersecurity ranking). The Integrated Electronic Case Management System (IECMS), covering the whole justice chain including police, was upgraded to a new micro-services architecture that went live in April 2025 with expanded functionality (e-court, enhanced case tracking). A 2023 University of Rwanda dissertation on rural Nyaruguru District confirms IECMS deployment and use in remote rural areas, alongside persistent ICT literacy and infrastructure barriers. Evidence supports Mostly digital - some paper given rural stations still face documented connectivity/literacy gaps despite a national digital-by-default policy.
revised_comments: Rwanda National Police stations, including those in rural areas, operate predominantly on digital systems as part of a sustained national digitisation drive. The Integrated Electronic Case Management System (IECMS), which covers the entire justice chain from police investigation through prosecution, courts and corrections, was upgraded to a new micro-services architecture that went live in April 2025, adding features such as e-court video conferencing and enhanced citizen case tracking. Driver testing and licensing are almost entirely digital, using Irembo-based booking and automated testing centres, and traffic enforcement uses automated speed cameras and digital fine systems. Rwanda ranks in the top tier of the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index. A university study of the rural Nyaruguru District confirms IECMS use in remote rural police and justice offices, though ICT literacy gaps and infrastructure limitations, including connectivity and computer access, mean some initial documentation still occurs on paper before digital entry.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Rwanda, primarily at the cell level (2148 cells covering rural areas), use the National Centralized and Integrated CRVS (NCI-CRVS) system for recording vital events like births and deaths at the point of service. For home births (common in rural areas), village chiefs complete paper community notification forms, which cell executive secretaries then enter electronically into NCI-CRVS within 30 days, generating a unique NIN and integrating with the National Population Register (NPR). Health facilities (rural included) have data managers who digitize maternity registers directly. Certification occurs via digital platforms like IremboGov. Law 32/2016 (revised 2020) mandates electronic registers, with paper used alongside for a transition period not exceeding 6 months, after which only electronic is used. Over 416 sectors and 2148 cells provide real-time digital services, contributing to high completeness rates (90%+ births in 2024). Digital systems are standard across rural facilities, but initial paper proofs persist, indicating some paper processes remain. No major barriers noted; strong government commitment and decentralization bridge national digital ambition with rural reality, though early transition (2020-2021) saw slight dips in completeness due to awareness and COVID.

revision_notes: Confirmed at 3. NIDA's Standard Operating Procedures confirm all civil registers have been maintained only in electronic format since 17 February 2020, per Law No. 06 of 2020, with the National Centralized and Integrated CRVS (NCI-CRVS) system in place at health facilities, cells, sectors, districts and embassies nationwide. Rwanda's 2025 Vital Statistics report shows birth registration completeness reaching 92.9% in 2025 (up from 90.3% in 2024), while death registration reached only 50.5% in 2025, leaving a substantial share of vital events, particularly deaths, unregistered or captured late. At rural cell offices, home births/deaths are first recorded on a paper community notification form by the village chief before the cell executive secretary enters the event electronically into NCI-CRVS within 30 days, meaning some initial paper capture persists ahead of the digital record. This mixed picture supports Mostly digital - some paper rather than fully digital.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Rwanda, based at the cell level, use the National Centralized and Integrated CRVS (NCI-CRVS) system, which has been maintained exclusively in electronic format since February 2020 under revised civil registration law. For births and deaths occurring in health facilities, registration is captured directly and digitally at the point of service. For events occurring in the community, common in rural areas, a village chief first completes a paper community notification form, which the cell executive secretary then enters into the electronic NCI-CRVS system within 30 days, generating a unique national identification number linked to the National Population Register. National birth registration completeness reached 92.9% in 2025, up from 90.3% in 2024, while death registration completeness stood at 50.5% in 2025. The system is decentralised to over 2,000 cells and 400 sectors, providing broadly consistent digital service, though reliance on an initial paper notification for community-based events means some paper handling remains part of the overall process.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Rwanda use digital systems like SDMS for enrollment, monthly attendance aggregates, and admin data; CA-MIS for assessment grades entry by teachers World Bank Learning Resilience Report. A 2025 mobile app enables daily digital attendance recording, rolled out to 2,371 schools across 22 districts including rural Nyamagabe, where teachers log attendance directly, generating real-time data New Times. Digital systems are standard (e.g., 85% teachers on CAMIS nationally), but paper may remain for daily details before monthly entry or in low-connectivity areas (56.7% schools connected, teacher-computer 14:1 primary). Pilots like OLPC in ~25% schools; national rollout indicates majority use. Barriers: rural connectivity gaps, device shortages, training. National EMIS ambition advancing, with rural reality catching up via recent apps and projects (Starlink, fiber). (148 words)

revision_notes: Confirmed at 3. The 2023/24 Education Statistical Yearbook (MINEDUC), drawing on the School Data Management System (SDMS), reports 97.4% of schools have at least one computer, a teacher-computer ratio improved to 2:1 (from 5:1 in 2017), and 61.8% internet connectivity, though only 35.5% of schools report using ICT directly in teaching and learning. A new mobile digital attendance application (Karame) was introduced from October 2025 and reached 2,371 schools across 22 of Rwanda's roughly 30 districts by December 2025, enabling real-time daily attendance capture and dropout-risk flagging as part of the Zero Out-of-School Children project; some schools reported data-matching issues during early rollout. Assessment data entry (CAMIS) and enrolment/aggregate reporting (SDMS) are established digital systems used by the large majority of schools, while daily attendance capture is only now shifting from paper to digital nationally, and connectivity/hardware gaps persist in some rural areas. This supports Mostly digital - some paper rather than a higher or lower score.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Rwanda use established digital systems for core administrative functions: the School Data Management System (SDMS) for enrolment and monthly attendance aggregates, and the Continuous Assessment Management Information System (CAMIS) for entry of assessment grades by teachers. As of the 2023/24 school year, 97.4% of schools had at least one computer and the teacher-computer ratio had improved to 2:1, though only around a third of schools reported actively using ICT in teaching and learning, and just under two-thirds had internet connectivity. From October 2025, a new mobile attendance application (Karame) began rolling out nationally, reaching 2,371 schools across 22 districts by December 2025, allowing teachers to record daily attendance digitally and enabling early identification of pupils at risk of dropping out, as part of the government's Zero Out-of-School Children initiative. Daily attendance recording is transitioning from paper logs to this digital tool but has not yet reached full national coverage, and some schools report data-matching issues during the transition. Connectivity gaps and device shortages remain barriers in some rural schools, but the overall direction is towards digital data capture with residual paper use during the transition period.
